guides.audience: Pastors, elder boards, and church leadership teams

guides.title: The Kingdom Turned Upside Down
guides.eyebrow: A five-session study on the Beatitudes and the blessed life.
guides.blurb:
This study is for Christians, seekers, and the small groups that carry them, who have heard the Beatitudes read at funerals and printed on wall art and never once felt their edge. It walks slowly through five sessions on the eight blessings Jesus pronounced from a hillside in Galilee, beginning with the word makarios itself and the strange fact that Jesus attaches blessing to exactly the people the world files under losing. It moves through the poor in spirit and those who mourn, the meek and those who hunger for righteousness, the merciful and the pure in heart, the peacemakers and the persecuted. And it keeps returning to the one thing most readings miss, that the Beatitudes are description before they are command, a verdict God speaks over the least likely people before they are a ladder anyone is asked to climb. It is built so a busy volunteer can lead it with no preparation. Every question carries the answer behind it. Every silence has a backup. Every session ends in prayer.

This is not a study that stands above the kingdom and hands out its requirements. The writer came to faith from atheism and was raised without a father, and he knows what it is to be the person the religious room had already counted out. He does not read the Beatitudes as the resume of the impressive Christian. He reads them as the door held open to the people who assumed they were disqualified, and he stands inside that door with everyone else, still poor in spirit on his best day. The one thing this study refuses, from the first session to the last, is to let the Beatitudes become eight new performances to grade yourself against. Jesus did not climb the mountain to raise the bar. He climbed it to announce that the kingdom of heaven had come near to the exact people the bar had always excluded. Blessed, he said, and he meant them.
guides.audience: Christians, seekers, and small groups

guides.title: The Long Obedience of Parenting
guides.eyebrow: A five-session study on parenting as formation, not performance, past the tips and into the cross.
guides.blurb:
This study is for parents, grandparents, and the small groups that carry them, who are tired of parenting taught as a set of techniques for producing an impressive child and want to know what the thing is actually for. It walks slowly through five sessions on formation against performance, on discipline that shapes a heart without dominating one, on a faith that cannot be handed down by force and the doubts a child must be allowed to own, on screens and attention and what a divided childhood does to a soul, and on the long and terrible mercy of letting go. It is built so a tired parent or a volunteer can lead it with no preparation. Every question carries the answer behind it. Every silence has a backup. Every session ends in prayer rather than in the guilt a parent already drove to group carrying.

This is not a study that stands above parenting and dispenses advice. The writer came to faith from atheism and was raised without a father, which means he began fathering with no map, no memory of a man who stayed, only a hole where the model should have been. He has five sons. He does not point from a safe distance. He has been the father who confused his child's performance with his own worth, who disciplined out of his own anger and called it correction, who tried to force a faith that can only be given, who let a screen become the easier thing to hand a boy, who gripped a growing son too tightly out of his own fear. He writes from inside the indictment. So will you. And the one place this study will not go, ever, is to tell a parent that the shaping of a child is a license to break one. Where discipline has become domination, where correction has become harm, there is no formation happening, only a wound being passed down, and the study says so plainly and points toward help. The rod in Scripture images a God who disciplines the ones he loves for their good and never for his rage. It was never a permission to crush a child in the name of raising one.
guides.audience: Parents, grandparents, and small groups

guides.title: The Love We Forgot
guides.eyebrow: A five-session study on friendship, loneliness, and the covenant of companions.
guides.blurb:
This study is for anyone who has more contacts than they have ever had and fewer friends than they can admit, and for the small groups willing to say so out loud. It walks slowly through five sessions on the love the modern world quietly demoted, on the loneliness that followed and the friendship C.S. Lewis said we stopped naming, on the covenant of David and Jonathan who bound their souls together in a court that wanted one of them dead, on the friend who wounds faithfully when a flatterer would have kept the peace, on the strange thing Jesus said the night before he died when he called his followers friends, and on the ordinary work of keeping a friendship alive in a mobile, distracted, exhausted age. It is built so a busy person or a volunteer can lead it with no preparation. Every question carries the answer behind it. Every silence has a backup. Every session ends in prayer rather than in the ache people already carried into the room.

This is not a study that stands above friendship and dispenses advice about it. The writer came to faith from atheism, was raised without a father, and knows the particular loneliness of the man who has learned to need no one. He does not point from a safe distance. He has been the friend who let the friendship starve because he was busy, who kept the acquaintance and lost the brother, who confused being surrounded with being known. He writes from inside the indictment. So will you. And the study will not pretend that friendship is a small thing you get to when the important loves are handled. Scripture calls friendship a love strong enough to knit two souls, faithful enough to wound, costly enough that the Son of God gave his life for his friends and then, astonishingly, called us that. We forgot it was a love at all. This study is the work of remembering.
guides.audience: Anyone carrying loneliness, and the small groups that meet honestly

guides.title: The Only Prayer Jesus Taught
guides.eyebrow: A five-session study on the Lord's Prayer, line by line, past the recitation and into the words.
guides.blurb:
This study is for anyone who has said the Lord's Prayer a thousand times and stopped hearing a single word of it, for the small group that wants to learn to pray and does not know where to begin, and for the skeptic who suspects the whole thing is a religious formula recited on autopilot. It walks slowly through five sessions, one for each movement of the prayer Jesus actually taught when his disciples asked him how to pray. It takes the address and the reverence, Our Father in heaven, hallowed be your name, and refuses to let either the intimacy or the awe swallow the other. It takes the two petitions that pray against your own preferences, your kingdom come, your will be done, and asks what it costs to mean them. It takes the request for daily bread and finds dependence and enough where we expected only groceries. It takes the terrifying conjunction, forgive us as we forgive, and does not flinch from the word as. And it takes the last petition and the doxology, lead us not into temptation but deliver us from evil, and ends where the prayer ends, on the kingdom and the power and the glory that were never ours. It is built so a busy person or a volunteer can lead it with no preparation. Every question carries the answer behind it. Every silence has a backup. Every session ends in the very prayer it studies.

This is not a study that stands above prayer and dispenses technique. The writer came to faith from atheism, was raised without a father, and is raising five sons, and every one of those facts sits inside the first word of this prayer. He does not point from a safe distance. He is the man who prayed with his mouth while his mind wandered to his calendar, who said Our Father for years before he could feel the word Father meant anything, who asked God to forgive him in the same breath he refused to forgive someone else. He writes from inside the indictment. So will you. And the one thing this study will not do is turn the Lord's Prayer into a technique for getting what you want from God, because the prayer Jesus taught spends four of its six petitions before it ever mentions your bread, and the whole thing is built to make you smaller and God larger, which is the opposite of what we came to prayer hoping to arrange.
guides.audience: New believers, seasoned Christians, seekers, and small groups learning to pray

guides.title: The Open Door
guides.eyebrow: A five-session study on hospitality, the stranger, and the table.
guides.blurb:
This study is for anyone who has confused hospitality with entertaining and wants to know what the thing actually is, and for the small groups and churches ready to practice it rather than admire it. It walks slowly through five sessions on the word Scripture uses, philoxenia, love of the stranger, which is not the same as the dinner party we throw for people who will throw one back. It sits with Abraham running to meet three strangers in the noon heat and the warning that some have welcomed angels without knowing it. It watches the table Jesus kept and the scandal of who he ate with. It looks at the early church as a household with an open door, and it ends where the reader lives now, with the lonely across the hall, the immigrant nobody wants, the outsider we would rather not seat, and the real cost of leaving the door open. It is built so a busy volunteer can lead it with no preparation. Every question carries the answer behind it. Every silence has a backup. Every session ends in prayer.

This is not a study that stands above the reader dispensing tips for a nicer gathering. The writer came to faith from atheism, was welcomed to a table before he believed a word of it, and knows what it is to be the stranger somebody made room for. He also knows the reflex to keep the door shut, to reserve the table for people like him, to call a clean house a good excuse and a busy week a mercy to himself. He writes from inside that reflex, not above it. And the study refuses two easy exits, the one that turns hospitality into a performance of a beautiful home, and the one that outsources the stranger entirely to a program so no actual stranger ever crosses an actual threshold. Hospitality in Scripture is not a spiritual gift for the extroverted and the well-decorated. It is a command, grounded in a God who set a table for enemies and welcomed us while we were still strangers to him.
guides.audience: Individuals, families, and small groups; useful for churches rethinking welcome

guides.title: The Open Hand
guides.eyebrow: A five-session study on generosity, contentment, and the heart that gives.
guides.blurb:
This study is for anyone who has quietly noticed that their fist is tighter than they wish it were, and for the small groups willing to look at money the way Scripture does, as a matter of the heart before it is ever a matter of the budget. It walks slowly through five sessions on the open hand as a spiritual thing before it is a financial one, on the widow's two coins and the accounting God actually keeps, on contentment as the soil that generosity grows in, on hospitality and the table as generosity with far more than money, and on cheerful giving as the freedom of a person who has stopped believing he owns his own life. It is not a study about tithing percentages or a household spreadsheet, and it is not about fixing an economy. It is about the grip, the one you cannot feel until you try to open it. It is built so a busy volunteer can lead it with no preparation. Every question carries the answer behind it. Every silence has a backup. Every session ends in prayer rather than in the guilt people already carried through the door about their money.

This is not a study that stands above the reader and passes the plate. The writer came to faith from atheism, was raised without a father, and is raising five sons on a pastor's income, and he knows the particular fear that makes a hand close. He does not point from a safe distance. He has been the man who called his tightfistedness stewardship, who gave the round number that cost him nothing and felt generous doing it, who lay awake counting a security that was never going to save him. He writes from inside the indictment. So will you. And the one thing this study refuses to do is turn the open hand into a new law to fail, a heavier weight laid on people already crushed, or a lever the prosperity teachers use to promise God will pay giving back with interest. Generosity is not a transaction that buys blessing. It is what a freed hand does. The open hand is not first a command. It is the shape a heart takes when it has finally believed it was given everything.
guides.audience: Individuals, couples, and small groups

guides.title: The Prayers We Were Never Taught
guides.eyebrow: A five-session study on suffering and lament, anchored in the Psalms and Job.
guides.blurb:
This study is for small groups, adult Sunday school classes, and individuals who have sat in a church that knew how to praise and did not know what to do with a person who could not. It walks slowly through five movements on suffering and the lost prayer the church forgot how to pray. It begins with lament as a vanished form, the cost of a worship that only ascends and never cries out. It moves into the lament psalms themselves, the how long of Psalm 13 and the unbroken dark of Psalm 88, the one prayer in the book that does not resolve. It sits with Job and the friends who explained too much, the failure of the tidy answer, the long silence in the ash. It comes to the cross, where God does not stand above the sufferer offering an explanation but climbs down inside the suffering and cries the lament himself. And it ends not in resolution but in a hope that refuses to be denial, the difference between an answer and a presence, between the question closed and the question carried.

This is not a study that will hurry anyone out of their grief. It will not hand a suffering person the platitude that everything happens for a reason, and the leader must never let it. Walter Brueggemann taught the church the cost of what he called the loss of lament, the price a community pays when it permits only praise. The Psalms gave Israel a language for the dark that the modern church has largely thrown away, and Job stands as the long protest God did not rebuke. The study holds the honesty of Psalm 88 without flinching. That psalm ends in darkness, and that is allowed. Most of all it implicates the leader and the writer. James Bell does not stand outside this. He was raised without a father, and he came to God out of atheism, and he has prayed prayers that got no answer he could see. He has stood at gravesides and had nothing to say that did not sound like a lie. He writes from inside the loss. So will you.
guides.audience: Small groups, adult Sunday school, and individuals

guides.title: The Rest We Refuse
guides.eyebrow: A five-session study on Sabbath, rest, and the God who stopped on the seventh day.
guides.blurb:
This study is for small groups, adult Sunday school classes, and individuals who are tired in a way that sleep does not touch, who suspect their exhaustion is not only a scheduling problem but a soul problem, and who have a vague guilt about rest they cannot quite name. It walks slowly through five movements on the Sabbath, on the God who rested when he did not have to, on rest as a refusal to be defined by what we produce, on the Lord who said the Sabbath was made for man and not man for the Sabbath, on what a day of actual rest looks like when you stop dressing your restlessness in spiritual language, and on the rest that still remains for the people of God. It leans on Walter Brueggemann's Sabbath as Resistance, on Abraham Joshua Heschel's The Sabbath, on Eugene Peterson, on Tim Keller, and on Dietrich Bonhoeffer, and it tries to earn every one of them rather than name-drop them. It is built so a busy volunteer can lead it with no preparation. Every question carries the answer behind it, every silence has a backup, and every session ends in prayer rather than advice.

This is not a study that will hand you a tidy schedule and call it holiness. It refuses the productivity sermon dressed as discipleship, the version of Sabbath that becomes one more thing to perform well. And it refuses the opposite error too, the spiritualized excuse that says rest is for the weak and the serious Christian grinds. Both are lies, and the leader must not let either win the room. Most of all it implicates the writer. Bell is terrible at this. He is a pastor whose one day off bleeds into hospital visits and half-answered emails, who has preached on rest with a phone buzzing in his pocket, who has called his inability to stop a calling. He came to faith from atheism, where work was the only god on offer and you were what you made. He was raised without a father, which taught him early that the weight was his alone to carry and no one was coming to lift it. He has five sons who needed a father who could stop, and a God who keeps inviting him to a rest he keeps declining. He writes from inside the refusal. So will you.
guides.audience: Small groups, adult Sunday school, and individuals

guides.title: The Self You Were Sold: Identity in a Self-Made Age
guides.eyebrow: A five-session study on who you are, walking out of the project of self-creation and into an identity that was given before it was ever performed.
guides.blurb:
This study is for small groups, adult Sunday school classes, and anyone exhausted by the work of being themselves. Not the work of a hard job or a hard week. The work of holding up a self you have to keep building, defending, updating, and selling, with no day off and no final version. It is for the person who has done everything the age told them to do, who has looked inward and found their truest self and become it and posted it, and who still lies awake suspecting that none of it is holding. And it is for the skeptic who has heard the church offer a thin answer to the deepest question a human being asks, who am I, and walked away unconvinced, and who deserves a better account than the one they were given.

The age we live in handed everyone a single instruction and called it freedom. Look inward. Find your true self. Define yourself, on your own terms, against every inherited expectation, and then become that self and present it to the world for approval. It sounds like liberation. For many it has become a sentence to hard labor, the labor of being your own author and your own audience at once, manufacturing a self from nothing and then anxiously watching to see whether it sells. This study walks slowly through how that self was invented, why it is so tiring, and what the older answer was before the modern one replaced it. Identity not as an achievement you assemble but as a gift you receive. Not the self you make, but the self you are given.

Bell does not write this from above. He came to faith from atheism, which means he spent years building a self with no God in the picture, looking inward for a foundation and finding sand. He was raised without a father, which means the question of who he was had a hole in the middle of it where an inherited name should have been. He has performed a self he was not sure was real. He has measured his worth by the room's reaction and gone home empty. He writes from inside the exhaustion, not at a clean distance from it, and the leader will lead from there too.
guides.audience: Small groups, adult Sunday school, and individuals

guides.title: The Stories That Undo You
guides.eyebrow: A five-session study on the parables and the kingdom they hide and reveal.
guides.blurb:
This study is for anyone who has heard the parables so often they have stopped hearing them, and for the small groups that want to be undone by the stories rather than merely informed by them. It walks slowly through five sessions on why Jesus taught in parables at all, a form built to reveal and to conceal at the same time; on the prodigal son and the older brother, the two lost sons of Luke 15 and the father who runs toward both; on the good Samaritan and the question a lawyer used to protect himself; on the kingdom parables, the mustard seed and the leaven and the hidden treasure and the sower, and the strange smallness of how God works; and on the parables of judgment and grace, the workers in the vineyard, the unforgiving servant, and the sheep and the goats. It is built so a busy volunteer can lead it with no preparation. Every question carries the answer behind it. Every silence has a backup. Every session ends in prayer.

This is not a study that stands above the parables and dispenses their meaning like a man handing out answers he settled long ago. The writer came to faith from atheism, and he remembers what it was to hear these stories as quaint and to be ambushed by them anyway. He reads them here as a pastor who has been every wrong character in them, the older brother nursing his ledger, the priest crossing the road, the servant forgiven a fortune and throttling a neighbor over pocket change. He does not point from a safe distance. He writes from inside the indictment, and he lets the stories do what Jesus built them to do, which is to get past the guard a plain command would trip, and to leave the hearer standing where he did not mean to stand. The parables were never illustrations that made a hard truth easy. They were traps for the conscience, sprung gently, that let a man judge himself before he knew he was the one on trial. Read them expecting to be caught.
guides.audience: Small groups, Sunday classes, and any reader willing to be caught by a story

guides.title: The Undivided Life
guides.eyebrow: A five-session study on following Jesus through an ordinary week.
guides.blurb:
This study is for small groups, adult Sunday school classes, and individuals who were handed a faith for Sundays and a calendar for the other six days, and who have lived in the gap between them so long they mistook the gap for adulthood. It walks slowly through five movements drawn from James Bell's book The Undivided Life, on the life lived in boxes and the one life offered whole, on marriage as covenant and the home that forms us, on the refusal to rest and the limits of the body, on all honest work as a calling, and on the rival god of money and the wholeness that is the real standard of a life. It is built to be run by a busy volunteer with no preparation. Every question carries the answer behind it, every silence has a backup, and every session ends in prayer rather than advice.

This is not a study about doing more. It is a study about being one person. The divided man is exhausted in a way he cannot explain to his doctor, because he is running several incompatible lives on the same set of bones, preaching generosity and hoarding, counseling patience and raging in traffic, believing God holds the future and lying awake managing it. The gospel offers, before it offers anything else, the rejoining of the man, one life surrendered to one Lord who is finally allowed to walk down the hallway and turn on the lights in the rooms we kept dark. And it implicates the leader and the writer first. Bell does not stand outside this. He came to faith from atheism and arrived with the convert's certainty that everything had changed, then discovered over slow years he had let almost nothing change in the places no one could see. He has lived in the boxes. He runs hot, confuses output with worth, has refused rest and called it devotion, has served the rival god and built a fortress called security. He writes from inside the dividing. So will you.
guides.audience: Small groups, adult Sunday school, and individuals

guides.title: The Unseen Battle
guides.eyebrow: A five-session study on the powers, the armor, and the war we cannot see.
guides.blurb:
This study is for Christians who suspect that the New Testament means something real when it says our fight is not against flesh and blood, and who are tired of choosing between two bad options, the church that finds a demon behind every bush and the church that has quietly stopped believing in the devil at all. It walks slowly through five sessions on the biblical worldview of the powers, on the armor of God read piece by piece, on temptation and the flesh that names the enemy within and not only the enemy without, on the victory already won at the cross where Christ disarmed the powers, and on the ordinary means by which ordinary Christians stand, prayer and Scripture and the gathered church and the table. It is built so a busy small group or a volunteer can lead it with no preparation. Every question carries the answer behind it. Every silence has a backup. Every session ends in prayer.

This is not a study that stands above the battle and reports on it. The writer came to faith out of atheism, which means he once held the materialist account of evil with both hands and knows its pull from the inside, the reasonable conviction that there is nothing behind the world but atoms and accidents. He also pastors real people and has watched things in a counseling room that the atoms do not explain. He writes from between the two errors C. S. Lewis named, the disbelief that flatters the enemy and the obsession that does the same. He will not sell you a war story to thrill you, and he will not talk you out of a war the Scriptures plainly describe. The one thing he refuses, on every page, is the sensational reading that turns a Christian into a frightened person scanning the room for spirits. The battle is real. The victory is already decided. And the weapons handed to the ordinary believer are almost embarrassingly plain, a belt, a shield, a book, a prayer, a shared loaf. This study means to put them in your hands.
guides.audience: Christians, small groups, and anyone unsure what to make of the New Testament's language of the powers

guides.title: The Water and the Table
guides.eyebrow: A five-session study on baptism and the Lord's Supper, on why God gives his people physical signs, and on the water and the meal that mark and feed the church.
guides.blurb:
This study is for new believers, membership classes, small groups, and any Christian who has taken the water and the bread for years without ever stopping to ask what they are. It walks slowly through five sessions on why Christianity, of all the world's faiths, refuses to be only a matter of the mind and insists on things you can touch, on baptism and the long, honest disagreement between those who baptize believers and those who baptize their infant children, on what baptism says about who you now are, buried and raised with Christ, on the range of ways faithful Christians have understood what happens at the Lord's table, and on the meal that was given to make a divided people one. It is built so a volunteer with no seminary training can lead it. Every question carries the answer behind it. Every contested point is stated in its strongest form before any verdict lands.

This is not a study that pretends the differences are not real, and it is not a study that treats them as walls. The writer is a Baptist pastor, and he says so plainly, and he still means to state the paedobaptist case and the range of views on the table so honestly that a thoughtful believer from the other side would finish feeling understood rather than beaten. He came to faith from atheism, carrying the modern instinct that the real world is only the world you can measure and that religion is something private and invisible, and he writes as a man the water and the table had to teach that God saves creatures with bodies through the good stuff of a world he made. The one thing this study will not do is let a second-order disagreement about the timing of a baptism or the metaphysics of a supper become the thing that divides the one body Christ died to make one. The mode of the water and the meaning of the meal are worth studying, worth deciding, worth holding with conviction. They were never worth breaking the table over.
guides.audience: New believers, membership and baptism classes, and small groups of any tradition

guides.title: The Weight You Carry
guides.eyebrow: A five-session study on faith, the mind, and the God who meets the desperate.
guides.blurb:
This study is for the person carrying a weight they cannot pray off, and for the small groups that want to sit with them without flinching or fixing. It walks slowly through five sessions on the Bible's own honesty about anguish, where the heroes of faith lie in the dirt and ask to die and are not rebuked for it, on the false choice the church keeps forcing between faith and therapy and between trust and medication, on anxiety as a thing the body suffers and not only a sin the soul commits, on the depression that is a dark night and not a moral failure, and on the church as a place where the crushed are carried rather than shamed. It is built so a volunteer with no clinical training can lead it, because every question carries the answer behind it and every session ends in prayer rather than in a diagnosis nobody asked for.

This is not a study that stands over the suffering and hands down cures. The writer came to faith from atheism, was raised without a father, and has sat under his own broom tree in the dark more than once, and he will not tell you what he has not lived. So he writes from inside it, not from a safe distance above it. And there are two lines this study will not cross, ever. It will never tell a suffering person that real illness is only weak faith, that the answer to a mind that will not quiet is to pray harder or believe better, because that is a cruelty with a Bible in its hand. And it will never pretend that a small group is a substitute for real help. Where there is danger, where a person is thinking of ending their life, the faithful thing is to get help now, and in the United States that means calling or texting 988, the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline, available every hour of every day. Therapy is grace. Medicine is grace. A doctor is grace. The God who made the body does not despise the mending of it, and neither will this study.
guides.audience: Anyone carrying anxiety, depression, or grief, and the small groups and pastors who walk with them

guides.title: The Work of Our Hands
guides.eyebrow: A five-session study on work and vocation, and the faith that has to survive Monday.
guides.blurb:
This study is for small groups, adult Sunday school classes, and anyone who has sat in a pew on Sunday feeling that their faith was real and large, and then walked into a job on Monday where it seemed to shrink to nothing. It is for the believer who suspects, somewhere underneath, that the real work of God happens on a stage with a microphone and that their own forty hours at a desk or a register or a job site are spiritually beside the point. It walks slowly through five movements on what work is and was meant to be, on Eden where God himself worked and called it good, on the thorns and the sweat that came after, on the lie that splits the world into sacred jobs and secular ones, on the idol that work becomes when it stops being what we do and starts being who we are, and on the strange promise that our labor is not finally lost. It is built to be run by a busy volunteer with no preparation. Every question carries the answer behind it, every silence has a backup, and every session ends in prayer rather than advice.

This is not a study that will tell you to find your passion and the rest will take care of itself, because most work is not passion and most weeks are not inspired, and the gospel has something to say to the ordinary Tuesday and not only to the calling that thrills you. It refuses two lies at once. The first says ordinary work does not matter to God, that only ministry counts, and the study takes that lie apart with Luther and Dorothy Sayers and the whole doctrine of vocation. The second says work is everything, the place we earn our worth and prove we exist, and the study names that as the idol it is. Most of all the study implicates the writer. Bell does not stand outside this. He is a pastor, and the pastorate is a job, a job he has loved into an idol, a job he has hidden behind, a job whose busyness he has called faithfulness when it was really fear. He has made the work of God a way of avoiding God. He writes from inside the problem. So will you.
guides.audience: Small groups, adult Sunday school, and individuals

guides.title: What Manhood Is For
guides.eyebrow: A five-session study on masculinity, strength, and the man Jesus was.
guides.blurb:
This study is for men who are tired of being handed two masculinities and told to pick, the swaggering one that mistakes volume for strength and the soft one that mistakes absence for peace, and who suspect the truth is neither. It walks slowly through five sessions on what biblical manhood actually is once the culture-war caricatures are cleared away, on the father wound and the God who names himself Father of the fatherless, on strength under control in the man who wept and washed feet and drove the money changers out with a whip, on emotional honesty and friendship and the silence that is killing men who will not say they are drowning, and on servant leadership against domination, and the calling every man has to raise or mentor the next one. It is built so a busy man or a volunteer can lead it with no preparation. Every question carries the answer behind it. Every silence has a backup. Every session ends in prayer rather than in the performance men so often bring into a room of other men.

This is not a study that stands over men and grades them. The writer came to faith out of atheism, was raised without a father, and is now raising five sons, and both of those last facts sit under every line. He knows the ache of a chair at the table that was always empty, and he knows the fear of a man who has no template for the thing he is trying to become for his boys. He does not write from a safe distance. He has been the man who confused controlling a room with leading it, who went silent for days rather than say he was afraid, who reached for anger because it felt more like strength than the truth did. He writes from inside the indictment, and so will you. And it refuses both counterfeits with equal force. It will not baptize the domineering man who reads Scripture as a permit for his temper, and it will not excuse the passive man who calls his absence humility. It holds up one man as the measure, the one who had all the strength there is and bent it entirely toward the good of the people in front of him.
guides.audience: Men, fathers, sons, and the small groups and mentoring pairs that carry them

guides.title: When Faith Has Questions
guides.eyebrow: A five-session study on doubt, deconstruction, and the God who is not afraid of either.
guides.blurb:
This study is for the believer whose faith has started asking questions the church taught him not to ask, for the small group that wants to talk about doubt without anyone reaching for the panic button, and for the skeptic who came along to be honest rather than to be fixed. It walks slowly through the hardest questions faith faces, the suffering that does not resolve, the God who hides, the Scripture whose reliability is contested, the hypocrisy that did real damage, the doctrine of hell, and the apparent quarrel with science. It refuses to win cheaply. Every hard question gets stated at its strongest before anyone answers it, because a faith that has to misquote the objection to survive it was never worth keeping.

This is not a study that shames the doubter or flatters him. The man who wrote it came to faith from atheism and was raised without a father, and he remembers the inside of the question, not just the answer to it. So the study draws a careful line, fairly and without contempt for either side. There is honest doubt that is faith asking God a hard question while refusing to let go of his sleeve, the doubt of the father who cried I believe, help my unbelief, and there is deconstruction that has already decided to leave and is only narrating the exit. The study respects both more than they expect. It will not pretend the leaver has no reasons, and it will not pretend the doubter is in danger of hell for doubting. It ends where Job ended and where Thomas ended, with a faith that has been through the fire, not a faith that never asked.
guides.audience: Skeptics, Christians with questions, small groups, and individuals

guides.title: When It All Comes Apart
guides.eyebrow: A five-session study on faith deconstruction, handled pastorally, for the person taking an inherited faith apart to see what is actually true.
guides.blurb:
This study is for the person pulling a faith apart piece by piece, for the friends and pastors who love them and do not know what to say, and for small groups willing to sit with hard questions without panicking. It walks slowly through five movements, on what you are actually taking apart when you say you are deconstructing, on whether doubt is a sin and the Bible's long line of honest doubters, on the wounds that come when the church itself is the reason, on rebuilding on rock rather than on the rubble of what you tore down, and on a faith small enough to be true and strong enough to hold weight. It is built to be run by a busy volunteer with no preparation. Every question carries the answer behind it, every silence has a backup, and every session ends in prayer rather than a verdict.

This is not a study that tries to talk anyone out of their questions, and the leader must never let it become that. Deconstruction is not a betrayal and it is not a fad. It is what an honest person does when the answers they were handed stop carrying weight. Many people taking their faith apart are not leaving Jesus. They are leaving a version of him somebody sold them, and the difference between those two departures is the whole question this study exists to help people see. Some of what gets torn down deserves to come down, the cultural baggage, the borrowed certainty, the politics dressed as the gospel. Some of what gets torn down is the load-bearing wall, and the cost of pulling it out only shows up later. The study holds both without flinching, and it refuses to make faithful sifting sound like abandonment or to make abandonment sound like courage. Most of all it implicates the writer and the leader. Bell does not stand outside this. He is a pastor, and pastors like him did the bundling, wrapping God and the institution and the politics into one package and handing it over as though it were all the same thing. He has watched people leave over what the church did and called it their unbelief. He has the questions too. So will you.
guides.audience: Those deconstructing, their friends and pastors, and small groups

guides.title: When It Does Not Make Sense
guides.eyebrow: A five-session study on suffering, lament, and the God who does not explain.
guides.blurb:
This study is for people in pain, for the ones sitting near them who have run out of things to say, and for the small groups willing to hold a hard question without rushing to close it. It walks slowly through five sessions on the problem of pain stated at full weight, on lament as faithful speech rather than faithlessness, on the cross as the place God answered suffering by entering it instead of explaining it, on the slow work endurance does without ever becoming a formula, and on the new creation where every tear is finally wiped away by the hand of God himself. It refuses the cheap answers the church reaches for out of its own discomfort, the everything happens for a reason and the God needed another angel, and it refuses just as firmly the despair that reads a wound as proof there is no one there. It is built so a person with no training can lead it, because every question carries the answer behind it, every silence has a backup, and every session ends in prayer rather than in the argument grief was already having on the drive over.

This is not a study that stands above suffering and dispenses answers. The writer came to faith out of atheism, was raised without a father, and has buried people he loved and sat with people who wanted to die, and he does not point at pain from a safe distance. He has prayed the prayer that was answered with silence. He has offered a grieving person the sentence he later wished he could take back. He writes from inside the room where the question why has no floor under it. So will you. And there is one thing this study will not do, ever. It will not tell a person in agony that the answer is simply to trust more, or that their grief is a failure of faith, or that God is fine with them staying in a darkness that is putting their life at risk. Where the pain has turned toward self-harm or despair that will not lift, the study says plainly that this is the moment to reach for a pastor, a counselor, a doctor, or a crisis line, and to reach today. The gospel does not require anyone to suffer alone. The God at the center of this study is the one who wept at a grave he was about to open.
guides.audience: Anyone in grief or pain, those walking with them, and small groups

guides.title: Where Is God When It Hurts: Suffering and the Goodness of God
guides.eyebrow: A five-session study on the problem of evil, the providence of God, and the hope that does not disappoint.
guides.blurb:
This study is for the person who has stood at a hospital bed, or a graveside, or in the wreckage of a marriage or a diagnosis, and asked the oldest question there is. If God is good, and God is able, why this. It is for the skeptic who left the faith over a child's cancer ward and was never given an answer worth the name, and for the Christian still inside the faith carrying a question the church kept handing them platitudes for. It is for the pastor who has run out of things to say at funerals. It does not promise to solve the problem of evil, because no honest book ever has, and the ones that pretend to are the ones that wound. It promises something harder and more durable. It takes the objection at its full and terrible strength, refuses every cheap answer, and walks toward the only response Scripture finally gives, which is not an argument but a Person who entered the suffering himself.

The five sessions move in order. First the question stated without flinching, the way the honest atheist states it, so well that the believer in the room feels it too. Then the doctrine of providence held without tidy resolution, a God who permits what he hates and works it toward an end we cannot see from inside it. Then the book of Job, where God answers the sufferer not with an explanation but with a whirlwind and a thousand questions, and rebukes the friends who had the formula. Then the cross, where the God who permits suffering does not stay outside it but enters it, bleeds inside it, dies inside it. And finally the hope that does not explain suffering away but defeats it, the resurrection and the new creation where every tear is wiped from every face. Bell does not write this from a safe distance. He came to God from atheism, and the problem of evil was the wall he could not get over for years. He has buried people he loved and prayed for healing that did not come. He is not solving a puzzle for you. He is standing in the rubble with you, pointing at the only light he has found that the dark could not put out.
guides.audience: Small groups, adult Sunday school, and individuals

guides.title: Where Your Treasure Is
guides.eyebrow: A five-session study on money, the heart, and the freedom Christ offers.
guides.blurb:
This is the small-group companion to James Bell's book Where Your Treasure Is, and it is not about the economy. It is about your heart and what it has quietly done with money. It walks slowly through five sessions on the heart that follows its treasure, the contentment we keep mistaking for resignation, the rich fool who confused a full barn with a safe soul, the anxiety that drives our reaching, and the strange freedom of the open hand. It is built to be run by a busy volunteer with no preparation. Every question carries the answer behind it, every silence has a backup, and every session ends in prayer rather than argument.

This is not a study that flatters the generous and indicts the greedy, because Bell does not believe the line runs there. It catches the man who gives and still grips, the woman who has little and still worships what she lacks, the giver who has used his giving to stop the question before it reached his heart. Most of all it implicates the writer. Bell does not stand outside this. He has lain awake doing arithmetic he called prudence. He has felt his chest loosen at a number in an account and called the loosening peace. He has loved his five sons and let the love become a reason to reach for more and never enough. He writes from inside the indictment about money, not above it. So will you. The question is never whether you may have money. The question is what your heart has done with it, and whether you can hear, under all the wanting, the voice of the One who became poor so that you could be free.
guides.audience: Small groups, adult Sunday school, and individuals

guides.title: Why We Still Need Each Other
guides.eyebrow: A five-session study on the church, the body of Christ, and the call to belong to a people who will let you down.
guides.blurb:
This study is for small groups, adult Sunday school classes, and anyone who has loved the church and been wounded by it in roughly equal measure, which is to say almost everyone who has stayed long enough to know what they are talking about. It walks slowly through five movements on what the church actually is, on the life together that Bonhoeffer described from inside a community that the state would soon scatter and kill, on the marks and the mess of a church that is a hospital of sinners and not a museum of saints, on the church sent into a culture that no longer assumes the faith, and on the hard grace of committing to a flawed people instead of leaving the moment they prove flawed. It is built to be run by a busy volunteer with no preparation. Every question carries the answer behind it, every silence has a backup, and every session ends in prayer rather than a tidy resolution.

This is not a study that defends the church by pretending it is fine. It will not do that, and the leader must never let it. The church has covered up abuse, baptized politics, traded its prophets for its donors, and bored a watching world half to death. The study takes all of that seriously and refuses to flinch. But it also refuses the easy exit, the conviction common to the wounded that the answer to a hypocritical church is no church, that a Christian can follow Jesus alone with a podcast and a Bible app. The New Testament knows no such Christian. Bell writes as a working pastor who has watched the church fail up close, who has been the failure more than once, and who loves her anyway, the way you love a family you cannot disown because it is the only family there is. He does not stand outside this. He has been the hypocrite in the pulpit. He writes from inside the body. So will you.
guides.audience: Small groups, adult Sunday school, and individuals

guides.title: Women of Valor
guides.eyebrow: A five-session study on womanhood, calling, and the image of God.
guides.blurb:
This study is for women who have wondered whether the church actually believes what Genesis says about them, for the men who have quietly assumed it was written for them, and for the small groups willing to read the whole canon instead of the same three verses. It walks slowly through five sessions, beginning with the dignity Genesis 1 gives every woman as the image of God and the way the fall distorted that dignity into rivalry and rule. It recovers the women the church forgot to teach, Deborah who judged Israel, Huldah who authenticated the word of God, Junia counted among the apostles, Phoebe who carried the letter to the Romans, Priscilla who corrected a preacher, Mary Magdalene sent to tell the men that Christ was alive. It takes the eshet chayil of Proverbs 31 back from the checklist it became and returns her to what the Hebrew says, a woman of valor, a warrior word. It reads the hard texts, First Timothy 2 and First Corinthians 14, and sets the complementarian and egalitarian readings side by side, each in its strongest form, before it lands. And it ends on calling in every season, single, married, mother, widow, worker, refusing to reduce a woman's worth to any one of them.

This is not a study written down to women from a safe height. It is written by a man, a pastor, a husband, the father of five sons, who has to confess at the outset that men built much of the church for men, that the sermons he grew up on quoted Paul's hard sentences to women and skipped the women Paul honored by name, that he himself has taught rooms as if half of them were furniture. He writes from inside that failure, not above it. And on the contested questions of what women may do in the church, the study refuses the cheap win in either direction. It states the complementarian case and the egalitarian case each the way its own best defenders would state it, sorts the matter honestly by how much it binds, and names where the author lands and the strongest objection he has not fully answered. A woman on the other side of that question should finish feeling understood, not beaten. The dignity is not up for a vote. The rest is held with an open hand.
guides.audience: Women, the men who worship beside them, and mixed or women's small groups

guides.title: You Become What You Repeat
guides.eyebrow: A five-session study on habits, desire, and the slow work of being formed.
guides.blurb:
This study is for anyone who has ever known the right thing and could not do it, who has stocked the head with correct belief and watched the life go on unchanged, and for the small groups tired of a discipleship that hands out more information to people who already have too much. It walks slowly through five sessions on the buried truth that a person is formed less by what she thinks than by what she loves, and that love is not a feeling that arrives on its own but a habit trained by practice. It looks honestly at the liturgies already forming us, the phone and the feed and the mall, and asks what they are aiming the heart at. It recovers the historic spiritual disciplines as counter-formation, the deliberate practices the church has always used to be re-aimed. It refuses the false war between grace and effort, showing that the disciplines are not earning but training. And it ends where it must, in a rule of life small enough that an ordinary person could actually keep it. It is built so a busy volunteer can lead it with no preparation. Every question carries the answer behind it. Every session ends in prayer.

This is not a study that stands above the reader and dispenses a technique. Bell came to faith out of atheism, argued his way in book by book, and assumed for years that he would be sanctified the same way he was converted, by getting his thinking straight, and he was not, and the gap between the theology he could pass a test on and the man he actually was is where this whole study was born. He writes from inside the failure. He is a pastor with a phone in his pocket that has formed him more than he wants to admit, a father of five sons who are learning what they love by watching what their father repeats. He does not point from a safe distance. And the one thing this study will refuse, at every turn, is the lie that formation is a performance you mount to earn God's favor. The disciplines are not the price of grace. They are how grace, already given, gets down into the muscles. We do not train to be loved. We train because we already are.
guides.audience: Individuals, small groups, and anyone tired of a faith that stays in the head
